en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Eight States of Horses as a Simile for Humans, translated from a separate version of the *Saṃyukta Āgama* by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
In a monastery where many bhikṣus were gathered together,
the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Horses have eight types of vicious behaviors."
What are the eight?
First, when the halter is loosened, it pulls at the carriage and wishes to bolt;
second, when harnessed to the carriage, it leaps and bounds, wishing to bite people.
The third posture was to lift both front legs and pull the cart as it ran;
the fourth posture was to tread upon the crossbar of the cart;
the fifth posture was to stand upright on two legs, grasp the yoke, rub it, and move the cart backward.
In its sixth state, it walks sideways and runs astray;
in its seventh state, it pulls the carriage and gallops away, until it finds muddy ground where it stops and refuses to go further;

in its eighth state, it hangs its head and stares at the fodder, refusing to eat; when its master leads it away intending to yoke it, it suddenly snaps and bites, desiring to eat but unable to get any food.
The Buddha said:
"A person also possesses eight types of corrupt and evil dispositions.
What are these eight?
The first type of person, upon hearing the sutra being preached, flees and does not wish to listen, like a horse that breaks its halter and yoke and pulls the carriage away as it runs.

The second type of person, upon hearing the sutra being preached, does not understand the meaning and does not know where the discourse is leading; they then become angry, leap about, and do not wish to hear, like a horse harnessed to a carriage that leaps about and attempts to bite people.
The third type of person, upon hearing the sutra being preached, immediately resists and refuses to accept it, like a horse that lifts its two front legs and pulls the carriage away as it runs.
The fourth type, upon hearing the sutra being preached, reviles it, like a horse that tramples the crossbar of a carriage;
the fifth type, upon hearing the sutra being preached, immediately rises and departs, like a horse standing on its hind legs, holding the yoke, rubbing itself, and backing away;
the sixth type, upon hearing the sutra being preached, refuses to listen, turning its head and looking askance while whispering, like a horse that walks sideways or runs astray.

The seventh state is when, upon hearing the preaching of the sūtras, one desires to challenge them with difficult questions; yet when questioned, one cannot provide a corresponding answer and instead dies committing false speech—like a horse that, having encountered turbid mud, stops and no longer proceeds.

The eighth state is when, upon hearing the preaching of the sūtras, one is unwilling to listen; instead, one dwells on lustful excesses and many worldly desires, refusing to receive the teaching. Only when about to enter the evil realms does one suddenly wish to study and practice the Path, yet by then one can no longer attain the practice of the Path—like a horse to which fodder is hung and offered, which stares at it but refuses to eat; when its master leads it away intending to harness it, the horse suddenly snorts and snaps, yet still cannot eat.
The Buddha said, "I have spoken of the eight vices of a horse; likewise, a wicked person also has these eight evil vices.
Having heard this sutra, the bhikṣus rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Eight States of Horses Compared to Humans.
